title: Life-sustaining cryobanking of human-scale organs

concept.text: The innovation is a reliable way to bank whole human-scale solid organs at cryogenic temperatures, then recover them for transplantation with function sufficient to sustain a recipient. Its defining capability would be an inventory of transplantable organs maintained for months or years, with acceptable injury after recovery and durable graft function after implantation. Human-scale life-sustaining recovery remains a goal in the supplied evidence.

The approach combines vitrification and nanowarming. Cryoprotectants help an organ enter a glass-like state during cooling, limiting damaging ice formation. Nanoparticles distributed through the organ’s vasculature generate heat internally during rewarming, addressing the difficulty of warming a large organ uniformly from its surface. Successful banking also requires preserving the organ through cryoprotectant loading and removal, cooling, storage, rewarming and restoration of circulation. Solving the heating problem alone does not establish transplantability.

significance.text: Donor-organ preservation currently imposes severe time constraints, usually measured in hours, although some approaches extend preservation into days. Reliable long-term banking would separate procurement from transplantation: organs could be collected into inventories, matched over time, transported with greater flexibility and implanted after recipient preparation. Scheduled procedures and a broader choice among stored organs would change transplantation from an immediate allocation emergency into a more planned clinical service.

The distinctive advance is the ability to maintain an inventory over months or years. Daytime surgery and wider geographic sharing are already partly enabled by shorter preservation extensions; those benefits alone do not establish the need for cryobanking. Long storage would additionally allow matching decisions to draw on organs procured at different times, rather than only those available during a short preservation window.

Greater use of scarce donor organs is a plausible downstream benefit, rather than a guaranteed direct outcome. Realizing it would require suitable allocation policies, safety assessment, banking infrastructure and clinical adoption. Banking could reduce losses caused by timing and logistics, but it cannot create an organ when no suitable donor exists. It therefore complements approaches that expand organ supply and does not by itself resolve the transplant shortage.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central remaining capability in the supplied studies is reproducible, sustained life-supporting transplantation after cryobanking at human scale. Rat kidneys have met a sole-organ survival endpoint, and a pig-kidney preprint reports human-scale recovery and acute transplant function. The next biological question is whether such large grafts can sustain recipients through the initial injury period, recover adequate filtration and maintain function over time. Urine production or short laboratory perfusion cannot answer that question.

Ice formation, thermal-stress cracking and cryoprotectant injury are distinct barriers. Nanowarming addresses the surface-heating bottleneck, but an organ still needs sufficiently uniform cryoprotectant and nanoparticle delivery and controlled cooling and warming throughout its tissue. Cryoprotectant toxicity and the injury associated with its delivery and removal remain important even when physical preservation appears successful. In the rat study, cryoprotectant damage was identified as the limiting factor for biological and functional recovery under the tested conditions.

Translation also requires acceptable vascular, tubular and filtration outcomes after reperfusion, followed by evidence about chronic tissue injury. Residual injury and reduced filtration in the pig experiments leave those questions open. Clinical-grade reagents and processes are another stated translational requirement. Success with one organ type would establish a starting point; different solid organs would still require their own preservation protocols and functional demonstrations.

current_state.text: A peer-reviewed study published in Nature Communications on June 9, 2023 demonstrated vitrification, storage for 1–100 days and nanowarming of rat kidneys followed by life-sustaining transplantation in male rats. All five nanowarmed syngeneic transplant recipients survived the planned 30-day study after removal of their native kidneys. The grafts therefore supplied the recipients’ renal support. Recovery included initial graft dysfunction followed by normalization of renal function; the result should not be read as immediate, injury-free recovery or as evidence of survival beyond the study endpoint.

The same group’s bioRxiv preprint, posted October 14, 2026, reports recovery of approximately 100-g pig kidneys, about 100 times the mass of the previously nanowarmed rat kidneys. Most kidneys in the perfusion experiments had been stored for 1–7 days. One kidney was stored at −150 °C for 366 days and then evaluated by normothermic perfusion, which circulates fluid through the organ at near-body temperature to assess function. The study reports vascular, metabolic and excretory recovery. The year-long storage result concerns one perfusion-assessed kidney and should not be generalized into a replicated year-long transplantation result.

Separate acute transplantation experiments in that preprint included three nanowarmed pig-kidney grafts, with three grafts per comparison group. The recipients retained their contralateral native kidney, and graft function was followed for 120 minutes in a non-survival experiment. The nanowarmed grafts produced urine immediately after transplantation, but residual injury and reduced filtration remained. These experiments establish surgical feasibility, reperfusion and immediate function under the tested conditions. They did not test whether the grafts could provide sustained, sole-organ renal support, and the preprint explicitly identifies survival transplantation as a required next step.

The supplied October 2026 version is a preprint and was not peer reviewed. The supplied review had complete main-article text for the rat study, but the retained pig-preprint extraction ended during page 50 and its figures were not visually inspected. The explicit methods and results summarized above were available within that extraction. These access limits constrain assessment of the entire preprint without negating the accessible experimental descriptions.

Evidence limitation: the supplied material contains no bounded freshness-search record establishing the field’s complete status as of November 1, 2026. It therefore cannot establish that no separate peer-reviewed pig-study publication, human transplantation or subsequent result existed by that date. Neither supplied study demonstrates human transplantation, and the pig study itself does not demonstrate life-sustaining recipient survival; broader claims of absence remain unresolved.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed initial demonstration: reproducibly preserve human-scale kidneys and at least one other solid organ below the glass transition for at least 30 days, then rewarm them with no detectable ice formation or cracking under prespecified assessments. The protocol should state detection limits and sampling coverage, since thermometry and imaging cannot establish the absolute absence of microscopic ice everywhere. These storage durations and organ requirements are proposed milestones, not established scientific or clinical standards.
completion_criteria.label: Human-scale organs reproducibly rewarmed after 30-day cryostorage without detectable ice or cracking

completion_criteria.text: Proposed functional demonstration: transplant the recovered organs into large animals after removal or elimination of the corresponding native organ function, so that recipient survival and the relevant physiological support depend on the graft. For kidneys, assessment should extend beyond urine production to sustained filtration, recovery from tubular injury and tissue outcomes. Prespecified survival and organ-function outcomes at 30 days should meet defined comparison margins against clinically relevant static cold storage controls. A nonsignificant difference alone would not demonstrate comparability.
completion_criteria.label: Recovered grafts sustain recipients with comparable 30-day survival and function

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility requirements: use sufficient independent organs and recipients to estimate success and failure rates, report initial dysfunction and unsuccessful recoveries, and reproduce the outcome across independent experimental runs and ultimately other centers. Organ-specific endpoints and comparison margins should be selected before testing. A second solid organ would demonstrate broader applicability, while finite experiments would establish the tested range of organs, sizes, storage conditions and protocols rather than universal applicability.
completion_criteria.label: Independent replication quantifies recovery outcomes and establishes tested applicability limits

completion_criteria.text: Proposed clinical progression: after convincing large-animal survival results and development of clinical-grade processes, an initial human series should demonstrate graft function within a prespecified range accepted for conventionally stored deceased-donor organs. Thirty-day storage and follow-up would be an initial milestone. Establishing the full months-to-years banking concept would additionally require replicated recovery after those longer storage durations and substantially longer follow-up for durable graft function, chronic injury and practical clinical use.
completion_criteria.label: Human grafts meet conventional-storage benchmarks after 30-day storage and follow-up

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis — SUR-02, Destination-therapy solid-organ xenotransplantation: xenotransplantation seeks a durable organ supply from another species, while SUR-03 seeks to preserve available organs until transplantation. The capabilities could complement each other if suitable xenografts could also be banked, but that combination would need direct testing. Cryobanking does not resolve the biological barriers to durable xenograft function.

Roster-based synthesis — SUR-12, Life-sustaining autologous solid organs assembled for implantation: SUR-12 addresses creating a patient-derived organ; SUR-03 addresses preserving an organ that already exists. A generated organ might eventually be banked, but preservation compatibility is a separate question. Neither organ assembly nor cryobanking establishes the other capability.

Roster-based synthesis — SUR-01, Operational donor-specific tolerance for the transplants patients actually receive: tolerance addresses the recipient’s immune relationship with a graft, whereas cryobanking addresses preservation and recovery. A well-preserved graft would still require an appropriate immune-management strategy. The syngeneic rat result, obtained between genetically matched animals, does not demonstrate donor-specific tolerance in the broader transplant population.

Roster-based synthesis — SUR-08, Reversible metabolic arrest after traumatic exsanguination cardiac arrest: both concepts concern recovering viable biological function after profound interruption of ordinary physiology. Their targets and demonstrations differ: SUR-08 concerns an injured whole patient during emergency rescue, whereas SUR-03 concerns an isolated organ stored cryogenically and subsequently transplanted. Success in organ vitrification would not establish reversible whole-body arrest.

Roster-based synthesis — SUR-09, Living, perfused autologous replacements for complex parts that grafts do not supply: both require preservation of living tissue architecture and circulation. SUR-09 concerns constructing replacements for complex parts, whereas SUR-03 concerns long-term storage and functional recovery of whole solid organs. Any extension of cryobanking to such replacements would require its own evidence.

change_log.change: Preserved the SUR-03 identity while explaining vitrification, vascular nanowarming and the complete preservation-to-transplantation sequence.
change_log.reason: The innovation concerns recoverable, life-sustaining organ banking; internal heating is one enabling component.

change_log.change: Narrowed the missing breakthrough to reproducible, sustained life-supporting transplantation at human scale.
change_log.reason: The pig preprint already reports human-scale physical recovery and acute function, so describing all human-scale recovery as missing would overlook reported progress.

change_log.change: Expanded the rat result with publication date, five syngeneic recipients, native-kidney removal, initial dysfunction and the planned 30-day endpoint.
change_log.reason: These details establish the strength and boundaries of the life-sustaining result without implying immediate normal function or longer-term durability.

change_log.change: Separated the single 366-day pig-kidney perfusion experiment from the acute transplantation cohort.
change_log.reason: The supplied review does not support implying that a year-stored kidney underwent transplantation or that year-long recovery was replicated.

change_log.change: Added the pig study’s approximately 100-g scale, usual 1–7-day storage, three nanowarmed transplant grafts, retained native kidney and 120-minute observation.
change_log.reason: These details distinguish immediate graft function from sustained sole-organ recipient support.

change_log.change: Replaced categorical assertions about absent human transplantation and absent journal publication with an explicit freshness limitation.
change_log.reason: The supplied record lacks a bounded search establishing those field-wide negatives at the cutoff.

change_log.change: Qualified hours-only preservation language and distinguished inventory-based matching from benefits available through shorter preservation extensions.
change_log.reason: The review recognizes hours-to-days alternatives and identifies months-to-years inventories as the distinctive capability.

change_log.change: Made improved organ utilization conditional on allocation, infrastructure, safety and adoption.
change_log.reason: Reliable preservation enables logistical flexibility but does not guarantee higher utilization or create donor organs.

change_log.change: Made completion criteria explicitly proposed, measurable and dependent on prespecified comparison margins, replication and organ-specific endpoints.
change_log.reason: Absolute absence of microscopic ice is not demonstrable by limited sampling, and nonsignificant differences do not establish equivalence.

change_log.change: Separated initial 30-day milestones from months-to-years storage and durable clinical graft survival.
change_log.reason: Shorter demonstrations cannot establish longer storage performance, long-term outcomes or universal applicability.

change_log.change: Removed revision-history wording and retained relevant extraction and figure-access limitations.
change_log.reason: Whether papers were reopened is not a scientific result; partial extraction and uninspected figures affect the scope of the supplied assessment.

change_log.change: Added distinct relationships to SUR-01, SUR-02, SUR-08, SUR-09 and SUR-12 using the supplied roster.
change_log.reason: These connections clarify complementary capabilities without merging concepts or assuming detailed specifications beyond their titles.

unresolved_issues: Whether a separate peer-reviewed version of the pig study, any human transplantation result or subsequent relevant evidence existed by November 1, 2026 remains unverified in the supplied material.
Whether human-scale cryobanked kidneys can sustain recipients without native renal support, recover from initial injury and maintain durable function remains unanswered by the supplied pig study.
The single 366-day perfusion result does not establish reproducible year-long banking or transplantation after year-long storage.
The pig-preprint extraction is truncated and its figures were not visually inspected in the supplied review, limiting assessment beyond the accessible text.

Acceptable injury limits, comparison margins, replication requirements, clinical process specifications and longer-term follow-up durations remain to be defined; the proposed milestones are not established standards.
The choice of a second solid organ and the extent to which preservation protocols transfer between organs remain open.
Related-concept relationships are based on roster titles because full specifications of those innovations were not supplied.
